title: The Edge of the Woods
sceneText:
Today’s ground runs out to the east side of the ducal woods. Hooves over the leaf litter, dull and regular.

Your eye goes along the far tree line. You know that direction. A little further north is the disputed boundary between Maplegate and Millridge.

From horseback that wood is no different from any autumn wood: dark brown, dark green, gold here and there.

Thierry rides beside you. His horse goes steadily. His eyes travel over different things from yours — he is looking at trunks, not at game.

“That wood of yours,” he says suddenly. “I measured it last month.”

variants.range_first:
He checks his horse and lets it slow.

“Good question,” he says. “Most people ask me how far my authority runs.”

He lifts his chin towards the north.

“My round ends at that slope. Beyond the slope is not somebody else’s; it is nobody’s. Undeclared woodland, nobody living there, and no road.”

“What makes a place have no road?”

“A place you get to by reading the ground,” he says. “There are a few old forest posts up there, built years back, not used now. Stone walls, half a roof, enough to keep the wind off. Two or three charcoal kilns as well, all abandoned.”

He pulls that much-folded sheet out of his coat — the map he drew himself — and opens half of it across the saddle.

“Hunters come through from that side in autumn. In winter there is nobody.”

He folds the sheet away.

“If you ever want to go, tell me. Do not go alone.”
variants.range_again:
He checks his horse.

“You asked me that before,” he says. “Let me think what I left out last time.”

He thinks about it as he rides, for a good stretch of the way.

“Those three places are not alike,” he says at last. “The easternmost one has a stone bottom. Clean, no mud comes off it, but no water either — you would be carrying it half a mile. The middle one is shaded; it does not see two hours of sun in a day. There is water, seeping down off the slope, and it does not freeze in winter.”

“The third I do not know well,” he says. “High. A good deal higher than the other two. There is a hollow up there. I have been once, in summer.”

“What was it like in summer?”

“Damp,” he says. “What grows up there is not what grows below. There are a few plants that will only live in a place like that.”

He glances at you.

“You are asking about this in a great deal of detail.”

You do not answer.

“Right,” he says. “I will not ask.”

effects.logEntry: You asked Thierry what he had measured in your wood.

choices.resultText:
“Thirty-seven of a size,” he answers straight away. “Nineteen of those are ready to come down. The rest are too young; give them another ten years.”

“That wood is not in bad heart,” he says. “It is only that nobody has managed it properly these last few years. Thinning wants doing yearly. Do it every other year and it stops being thinning and becomes cutting trees down.”

He turns his head to look at you.

“If you are still here next year I can set you out a five-year table.”

“If I am still here next year,” you say.

“Yes,” he says. Easily, without a pause. “If you are still here next year.”

choices.text: Bring up the skid road on the Millridge side

effects.logEntry: You brought up the skid road with Thierry from the saddle.

choices.resultText:
“I know that road,” he says. “I have walked it too.”

You wait for him to go on. He does not.

Another stretch of the way, and then he speaks.

“The sentence you want out of me, I cannot say here.” He lifts his chin at the field ahead. “That man up front is Millridge’s.”

He does not look round at you.

“In the woods I can say it. Not here.”

choices.text: Ask how much of this country lies outside his round

effects.logEntry: You asked Thierry how much of the country lay outside his round.
